Why do magnetic field lines never intersect, unlike some electric field lines in complex charge distributions?

options.text: The field direction would be ambiguous at the intersection

text_solutions: Magnetic field lines represent the direction of the magnetic field at each point. If they intersected, it would imply two different directions for the field at the same point, which is physically impossible. This uniqueness stems from the vector nature of the magnetic field and the absence of magnetic monopoles.

text_solutions: Soft ferromagnetic materials have low coercivity and do not retain significant magnetization after the external field is removed. qns_content.text: A magnetic dipole placed in a uniform magnetic field experiences no net force but a torque. This is because:

options.text: Forces on the poles cancel out but produce a couple
The field exerts a net force in one direction
The dipole is inherently unstable in uniform fields
The field strength varies across the dipole

text_solutions: In a uniform magnetic field, the forces on the north and south poles of a dipole are equal and opposite, canceling out to produce no net force. However, these forces act at different points, creating a torque that tends to align the dipole with the field.

qns_content.text: The absence of a net force on a magnetic dipole in a uniform field implies:

text_solutions: In a uniform magnetic field, the forces on the dipole’s poles are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, resulting in no net translational force. This occurs because the field strength does not vary, unlike in a non-uniform field where a gradient would produce a net force.

qns_content.text: Unlike a bar magnet, an iron nail near a magnet experiences both a net force and a torque. This is primarily due to:

The cancellation of forces on the nail

text_solutions: An iron nail, being a ferromagnetic material, becomes magnetized in the non-uniform field of a bar magnet, developing an induced magnetic moment.
